title: Understanding the AI economy
gist: Google released ATLAS v1.0, a study built on 15 million de-identified human-AI interactions across the Gemini App, AI Mode and the Gemini API, covering 150+ countries, 800 occupations and 4,000 tasks. The headline findings cut against the automation narrative: AI touches 68% of US occupations but only ~21% of tasks within a typical job, under 10% of work interactions fully automate a task, and over 86% of all usage happens outside work entirely.

insights.claim: Google's AI & Economy ATLAS v1.0 dataset is built from 15 million aggregated, de-identified human-AI interactions drawn from the Gemini App, AI Mode and the Gemini API, products Google says are collectively used by more than 1 billion people monthly.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: First vendor-scale disclosure of Gemini's real usage base and mix — a rare hard denominator for sizing Google's consumer AI footprint against OpenAI and Meta.
insights.quote: ATLAS’s first dataset (v1.0) is built from 15 million aggregated and de-identified human-AI interactions across the Gemini App, AI Mode, and the Gemini API, which together are used by more than 1 billion people monthly.
insights.locator: To help, Google is launching the first iteration

insights.claim: ATLAS v1.0 coverage spans more than 150 countries, 140 languages, 800 occupations and 4,000 tasks, which Google positions as the most comprehensive empirical view of AI usage published to date.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: Sets the benchmark other labs' usage studies will be compared against; the occupation/task taxonomy is the layer where labor-displacement estimates get built.
insights.quote: ATLAS is the most comprehensive look to date at how real people are using AI at scale.
insights.locator: ATLAS v1.0 insights span more than 150 countries

insights.claim: ATLAS is powered by Google DeepMind's Observation Clustering and Taxonomy Organisation (OCTO), a tool that converts massive unstructured LLM conversation text into organized entities.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: Signals Google has an internal conversation-mining stack that could become a product or policy-influence asset, not just a research artifact.

insights.claim: Google routed the ATLAS v1.0 report through outside economists — Dame Diane Coyle of Cambridge and Dr. David Autor of MIT — rather than publishing usage statistics purely in-house.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: Enlisting the two most-cited labor economists on automation is a regulatory-positioning move; expect ATLAS numbers to surface in policy debates about AI and jobs.
insights.locator: We'd like to acknowledge Dame Diane Coyle

insights.claim: Google's ATLAS data shows workplace AI adoption reaching 68% of all occupations representing 90% of total U.S. employment, but within a typical job AI is used for only about 21% of tasks.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: Penetration is nearly saturated by headcount but shallow by task — the remaining ~79% of tasks is the addressable runway that justifies further seat-based AI monetization.
insights.quote: in a typical job AI is used for only ~21% of tasks
insights.locator: AI use at work is broad but shallow

insights.claim: Google frames current enterprise AI diffusion as 'broad but shallow,' meaning breadth of adoption is a misleading proxy for depth of workflow integration.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: A useful lens for discounting vendor adoption stats: track task-share, not seat-count, when underwriting AI software revenue durability.
insights.quote: AI use at work is broad but shallow
insights.locator: AI use at work is broad but shallow

insights.claim: Less than 10% of workplace AI interactions in ATLAS fully automate a task; the vast majority are collaborative uses such as ideation, strategy, information retrieval and learning.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: Undercuts near-term mass-displacement theses and supports pricing models tied to augmentation seats rather than headcount replacement.
insights.quote: Less than 10% of those interactions fully automate tasks.
insights.locator: At work, most AI use is focused on collaboration

insights.claim: Non-routine cognitive tasks such as creative design and hypothesis testing appear in AI work interactions at 65% versus 35% in the economy as a whole, meaning AI usage is skewed toward exactly the work previously assumed hardest to automate.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: Inverts the classic routine-task-bias model of automation; sectors whose value is creative and analytical judgment are the earliest, not the latest, to be exposed.
insights.quote: show up in AI work interactions at a much higher rate than in the economy as a whole (65% vs 35%)
insights.locator: Tasks like creative design and hypothesis testing

insights.claim: Workers in manual and technical trades — auto technicians, industrial mechanics — use conversational AI as a live collaborator for real-time diagnostics, troubleshooting and on-the-fly learning, contradicting the assumption that AI adoption is a knowledge-work phenomenon.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: Opens a field-services and trades software TAM that consensus AI adoption models largely ignore.
insights.locator: AI use is not limited to white collar workers

insights.claim: Workers in manual and technical trades are 2x more likely than other users to use multimodal AI — generating or interpreting images and video — when they use Google's AI tools.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: Multimodal inference is far more compute-intensive per query than text; a trades-led adoption wave shifts the serving cost mix and favors vendors with cheap vision inference.
insights.quote: they’re 2x more likely to use multimodal AI
insights.locator: AI use is not limited to white collar workers

insights.claim: Over 86% of all AI interactions captured in ATLAS occur outside of work, meaning the large majority of AI's realized utility sits in household activity that standard economic metrics do not capture.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: If most AI value is consumer surplus rather than measured output, productivity statistics will lag the technology badly — a reason to distrust GDP-based AI ROI debates.
insights.quote: Over 86% of interactions with AI tools in ATLAS occur outside of work.
insights.locator: AI is delivering value at home

insights.claim: High-friction administrative tasks — navigating government services such as taxes, licensing and fines — are a named consumer AI use case in ATLAS, alongside productive household activity like researching purchases and operating appliances.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: Identifies govtech and consumer-transaction intermediation as concrete monetizable AI surfaces, and a disintermediation risk for tax-prep and form-filling incumbents.
insights.locator: AI is delivering value at home

themes.theme: Global diffusion and the digital divide

insights.claim: ATLAS records AI usage across more than 150 countries and territories representing 99% of the world's population, but on a per-capita basis usage closely mirrors a country's relative wealth.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: AI intensity is tracking GDP per capita rather than leapfrogging it — bearish for the thesis that AI compresses development gaps, and a policy hook for subsidy programs.
insights.quote: on a per-capita basis AI usage closely mirrors a country’s relative level of wealth, raising concerns about a persisting digital divide
insights.locator: Global AI adoption is tracking GDP per capita

insights.claim: Some middle-income countries in South America and the Middle East are adopting AI at rates comparable to higher-income countries, breaking the otherwise tight link between wealth and AI usage.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: Flags specific emerging markets where AI consumption is running ahead of income — the near-term growth pockets for consumer AI monetization outside the OECD.
insights.locator: However this isn't a universal rule

insights.claim: English accounts for only about a third of global AI conversations in ATLAS, and users do not systematically switch away from their native languages even for complex tasks.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: Multilingual quality is a competitive moat rather than a nice-to-have; models weak outside English are structurally capped at roughly a third of the interaction pool.
insights.quote: English represents only about a third of global AI conversations, and users do not systematically abandon their native languages for complex tasks.
insights.locator: Global AI adoption is tracking GDP per capita

insights.claim: ATLAS v1.0 excludes Google Workspace, Google Translate and AI Overviews, plus enterprise platforms Gemini for Google Cloud and Gemini Enterprise, and frontier areas such as agentic coding and world models — so the 15 million interactions understate Google's total economically-relevant AI usage.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: The excluded list is effectively Google's enterprise AI product map; whichever of these appears in ATLAS v2 signals where Google now has usage worth showing.
insights.locator: And there is a much wider range of economically-relevant AI usage

insights.claim: Google presents ATLAS as an ongoing long-term study whose scope will expand, run through its AI & Economy Research Program in collaboration with academic researchers, rather than as a one-off publication.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: Creates a recurring, comparable time series on AI task penetration — a tradeable leading indicator for AI software demand if the ~21% task-share figure starts moving.

insights.claim: Google argues AI's economic outcomes are neither automatic nor guaranteed and require deliberate collective shaping informed by empirical evidence, framing its own usage data as the input to that process.
insights.speaker: Zanna Iscenko
insights.so_what: A vendor supplying the primary evidence base for AI labor policy is a soft-power position worth tracking as regulation is drafted.
insights.quote: the outcomes – what this means for work, for people’s lives, and the economy writ large – are not automatic nor guaranteed
